en.commentary: ElevenLabs keeps the crown in 2026, and the gap to second place is smaller than it has ever been. Turbo v2.5 holds the realism lead and Eleven v3 covers 74 languages with inline emotion tags, but Hume's Octave 2 model arrived this spring with genuine emotional intelligence at 58% lower per-character cost, and that combination is hard to beat for narration work where the script carries feeling. Cartesia and OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts split the lower-half of the table for completely different reasons: Cartesia's 90ms TTFA owns the voice-agent use case, and OpenAI's $0.015 per minute price kills every other API on raw cost for batch jobs. Murf and WellSaid still matter for compliance-bound enterprises, but for individual creators, podcasters, and indie developers in 2026, the real fight is ElevenLabs versus Hume on price-to-quality and Cartesia versus OpenAI on price-to-latency.

highlights.title: ElevenLabs is still the safe default for serious voice work
highlights.body: Turbo v2.5 sits at 75ms latency and Eleven v3 reads inline emotion tags across 74 languages, which means you can ship the same script in Mandarin, Spanish, and Japanese without re-recording. The $5 Starter plan unlocks Instant Voice Cloning, and Professional Voice Cloning at $22 is the bar everyone else is benchmarked against.

highlights.title: Hume AI Octave 2 is the smartest move for narrators in 2026
highlights.body: Octave 2 reads emotional context from the script itself rather than waiting for SSML tags, and Hume's per-character pricing comes in 58% under ElevenLabs at the Business tier. The $14 Creator plan ships unlimited voice cloning, which is the most aggressive cloning entitlement in the category.

highlights.title: Cartesia Sonic 3 owns voice agents under 100ms
highlights.body: Sonic 3 hits 90ms TTFA with the Turbo variant at 40ms, and a 3-second audio sample is enough for a usable clone. At $0.030 per minute on the API, anyone building a real-time conversational agent in 2026 should benchmark against Cartesia first and only move on if they have a specific reason.

highlights.title: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts wins on raw economics for batch work
highlights.body: $0.015 per minute is half what most competitors charge, and the 13 voices are steerable through plain-English instructions rather than markup. For audiobook back catalogs, language-learning content, or any high-volume pipeline where you control the script, this is the API to start with.

highlights.title: WellSaid and Murf still win the enterprise stack
highlights.body: WellSaid's SOC 2 plus ISO 27001 certifications and Murf's native Canva, PowerPoint, and Google Slides integrations are the reason Fortune 500 L&D teams keep paying $49 to $199 per month per seat. ElevenLabs has the better voices, but enterprise procurement and brand consistency live and die on the workflow integrations these two have built.

en.commentary: ElevenLabs is the only top-tier voice provider shipping at a steady cadence right now and it shows. The May release notes added SAML SSO on iOS and Android for enterprise tenants, multimodal message support inside hooks, audio duration metadata in speech-to-text responses, the no_verbatim transcription flag for cleaned-up output, and Scribe realtime keyterms biasing on WebSocket. Add the IBM agentic AI partnership announced March 25 and the v3 platform that now integrates voice, music, and Scribe under one stack, and the moat keeps widening. I'm bumping language support a tenth on the back of fresh font-rendering coverage for Hebrew, Thai, Armenian, Georgian, Malayalam, Telugu, and Gurmukhi; that detail matters more than it sounds when you're shipping voice into Asia or the Middle East. Hume Octave-2 stays at second because emotional range at 9.7 still leads the category. Minimax 02 HD remains the best multilingual mid-tier pick at $0.10 per 1M characters. Cartesia Sonic-3 is the right call when latency is everything: real-time voice agents, customer support, and live translation are its territory and 9.9 latency reflects that. OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts is the value floor for anyone already paying for the OpenAI API. Murf and WellSaid are the corporate e-learning incumbents. The pattern is clear: ElevenLabs is the safe enterprise pick, Hume is the expressive narration pick, Cartesia is the latency pick, and Minimax is the multilingual budget pick. Resemble and Descript Overdub are useful for editing-first workflows but no longer competitive on raw realism.

highlights.body: The March 25 announcement of premium voice for IBM agentic AI puts ElevenLabs inside the largest enterprise procurement pipeline in the industry. Expect Fortune 500 deployments to follow.

highlights.title: Cartesia is for real-time agents
highlights.body: 9.9 latency makes Sonic-3 the only credible pick when the use case is a live voice agent or simultaneous translation. Latency below human reaction time changes what you can build.

highlights.title: Multilingual budget tier is settled
highlights.body: Minimax 02 HD at $0.10 per 1M characters with 9.2 language support is the obvious choice for anyone running multilingual content at scale without enterprise budget.

en.commentary: I recorded a Mother's Day card from my dad to my mum over the weekend, English to Mandarin, and the test ran through every voice model on this list. ElevenLabs is still first because it is the only system where the cross-lingual clone preserves my dad's tonal habits convincingly, the v3 update last quarter is still the line nothing else has crossed for personal-voice work. Hume Octave 2 at two is the right choice when emotion matters more than likeness, the prompt-driven emotional range is genuinely a different feature from anything ElevenLabs ships, and for audiobook narration or anything dialogue-heavy I would pick it without hesitation. MiniMax Speech 02 HD stays at three, the Asian language support is the best in the top tier and the latency is competitive for live agent work. Cartesia Sonic 3 owns latency at 9.9, if you are building a voice agent and every millisecond matters this is the model, the trade-off is a slightly less expressive voice. OpenAI's GPT-4o mini TTS at five is the value play, the price drop last month made it the default for any product where good-enough voice at scale is the requirement. Below those five the field is mostly serving specific verticals, WellSaid for studio-quality narration, Murf for corporate explainers, Speechify for accessibility. Descript Overdub at ten is fine for podcast cleanup but I would not start a new project there in 2026.

highlights.title: ElevenLabs is the only voice clone I trust with my own family's voices

highlights.body: 9.7 on emotional range is the highest in the category and it shows up in audiobook work where pacing and feeling matter more than literal voice match. For narrative content this is the model I default to.

highlights.title: Cartesia Sonic 3 owns sub-100ms latency
highlights.body: Building a real-time voice agent and every millisecond counts? Sonic 3 at 9.9 latency is the answer, the trade-off in expressiveness is acceptable when interactivity is the product. Nothing else in the field is close on response time.

highlights.title: OpenAI's mini TTS is the default for shipping at scale
highlights.body: GPT-4o mini TTS at 9.6 value for money is the obvious choice when you need decent voice across millions of generations. The recent price drop made this category economics work for products that previously could not afford TTS at all.

zh-tw.commentary: 母親節週末我幫爸爸錄了一張給媽媽的語音卡片，英文翻成中文那種，順便把這份榜單上每個模型都跑一輪。ElevenLabs 還是第一，老實說它是唯一一個跨語言複製還能把我爸的語氣習慣保留下來的工具，上一季 v3 更新拉開的差距到現在沒人跟上，個人語音克隆這件事它就是領先一條街。Hume Octave 2 排第二，情感比像更重要的時候選它，prompt 直接給情緒這個功能 ElevenLabs 還做不到，有聲書或對白量大的腳本我自己一定用它。MiniMax Speech 02 HD 第三穩穩的，亞洲語系支援在頂級這層是最強的，延遲也夠跑即時對話。Cartesia Sonic 3 在延遲 9.9 是場上唯一，做 voice agent 在意毫秒的人就選它，代價就是聲音表現力稍微平一點。OpenAI GPT-4o mini TTS 第五是 CP 值之王，上個月降價後產品要大量產出語音預設就選它。後面五名各有專長，WellSaid 做錄音室等級旁白、Murf 做企業簡介、Speechify 做無障礙閱讀。Descript Overdub 排最後做 podcast 修補還行，2026 年從零開始的新專案我自己不會挑它。

en.commentary: ElevenLabs holds the top spot and the v3 multilingual update that shipped this week tightens its lead on Cantonese, Vietnamese, and Polish, which were the three languages where serious competitors could close the gap. Hume AI Octave 2 expanded emotional control to 32 dimensions and stays at second because emotional range is genuinely category-leading for any narrative or game-dialogue use case. Cartesia Sonic 3 hit 200ms first-token latency on edge deployments this week, which is the kind of number that wins real-time voice agent work, and it moves up a position. For any voice agent that needs to interrupt and resume naturally, Cartesia is now the right pick. MiniMax holds third for multilingual general-purpose work. OpenAI GPT-4o-mini-TTS is still the right default for budget-conscious indie projects. Murf, WellSaid, and Speechify are unchanged. The market is bifurcating into a quality tier (ElevenLabs, Hume) and a latency tier (Cartesia, OpenAI), with MiniMax bridging both, and I expect that split to deepen through summer.

en.commentary: Inworld and ElevenLabs are sharing the top of my chart again this week, and both earned it for different reasons. Inworld's TTS-1.5 Max still sits at the top of the Artificial Analysis Speech Arena with an ELO around 1236, winning blind tests for naturalness and conversational flow, and its sub-250ms P90 latency on Max is what real-time agents actually need. The bigger story is that Inworld just previewed Realtime TTS-2, a model built specifically for live conversation. It hears the full audio of an exchange, picks up the user's tone and pacing, and takes voice direction in plain English the way you would prompt an LLM, all while holding one voice identity across more than 100 languages. That is a genuine step toward voice agents that feel like people, and it is why Inworld keeps the number one slot. ElevenLabs stays right beside it because nothing beats it for creator tooling and cloning fidelity. Eleven v3 now covers 70-plus languages, adds inline Audio Tags for emotional direction, and cuts errors on complex text by about 68 percent versus v2, which is exactly what audiobook and video producers want. On price, Inworld is the disruptor at roughly 5 dollars per million characters against ElevenLabs at 30 to 60, so budget-driven teams have an easy answer. I am holding the rest of the order steady. Hume's Octave 2 keeps third for its emotional range, MiniMax and Cartesia stay strong for multilingual and ultra-low latency work, and OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini-tts remains the value pick for developers already in that ecosystem. The takeaway this week is that real-time conversational quality has become the battleground, and Inworld is setting the pace.

en.commentary: ElevenLabs and Inworld stay locked together at the top, and this week's news only sharpens why ElevenLabs holds the edge. The May 7 platform reset cut TTS prices by up to 55 percent, which finally fixes the one complaint I always had about it. With Eleven v3 already shipping audio tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and 74 languages, the value-for-money gap that used to favor cheaper rivals has basically closed, so I am nudging its value score up. Inworld remains my pick for real-time agents where its latency is simply the best in class. Cartesia deserves a small bump too. Sonic-3 landed in April and a Sonic-3.5 update is now rolling out, with time-to-first-byte driven under 100 milliseconds, which is exactly what live voice applications need. I am edging Cartesia ahead of MiniMax this week on the strength of that real-time lead, though the two are close enough that your choice should come down to whether you need raw speed or broader language coverage. Hume Octave still owns emotional range and stays third for any project where the voice has to convey feeling rather than just read text. For most buyers the map is clear. ElevenLabs for the best overall voice now that pricing is fixed, Inworld or Cartesia for low-latency agents, Hume for emotion, and OpenAI's mini TTS when you want steerable, instructable voices on a budget.

Cartesia Sonic 3 stays fourth and remains the realtime realism leader, with a Sonic 3.5 update rolling out through May that keeps its near-instant time-to-first-byte the benchmark for conversational use. That is a genuine, dated launch rather than a vibe. en.commentary:
The headline number this month is from the Artificial Analysis Speech Arena: in blind tests, over 58% of listeners failed to correctly pick out the synthetic speaker when using current top models. Realism has arrived. The buying decision has moved to latency, emotional control and how many languages you actually need.

ElevenLabs stays first. Eleven v3 has been generally available since February with 70+ languages and audio tag controls, and the tag system is the reason I keep paying: writing a bracketed instruction for a whisper or a laugh is faster than re-recording a take. The company added a $990/month Business tier and is reportedly in talks at around a $22B valuation, which tells me the enterprise side is funding the research.

I moved Cartesia up to third this week. The latest Sonic release posts a time to first audio around 40ms, a new benchmark for real-time dialogue, and if you are building a phone agent or a live translator, that number is the entire product. Nothing else here answers that fast, so its perfect 10 on latency now carries a rank with it.

Hume sits fourth at 8.9. Octave 2 still holds the highest emotional range score in this ranking at 9.7, and steering delivery with plain English instructions instead of SSML parameters is a genuinely nicer way to work. Worth knowing that founder Alan Cowen and core researchers moved to Google DeepMind in January to work on Gemini voice, so I am watching the shipping pace here.

Inworld holds second on the strength of near-Cartesia latency with much richer expression. For a game NPC or an interactive character, that balance is the one I would build on.

en.commentary: ElevenLabs keeps my top spot and this month's listening tests back it up. Its v3 engine scores around 89.6 percent on naturalness in independent testing, and its output passes blind listening tests against human voice actors for most narrative content. With a 9.7 voice-realism score and the broadest language coverage in the field at 9.8, it is the one I recommend for audiobooks, dubbing, and any project where a listener should never suspect a machine. Inworld TTS 1.5 Max stays tied at the top of my scores and it is the pick when latency matters as much as quality. Its 9.8 latency score and near-top realism make it the smoothest choice for real-time agents and interactive apps. Cartesia Sonic 3 holds third on the strength of a perfect 10 latency score, and it is still the fastest end-to-end voice I test, ideal for live conversational systems where every millisecond of delay is felt. Hume AI Octave 2 sits fourth as the emotion specialist, with a field-best 9.7 emotional-range score that makes it the choice when content needs genuinely conveyed feeling. Fish Audio's OpenAudio S1 rounds out the top five on outstanding value at 9.8, the pick for high-volume work on a budget. No new model launched this week to reorder the leaders, so ranks hold. The category has specialized cleanly: ElevenLabs and language breadth lead on quality, Cartesia and Inworld on latency, Hume on emotion.

en.commentary: ElevenLabs holds the top spot because it remains the default the whole category is measured against. Its Eleven v3 model went generally available in February with explicit audio tags across 70-plus languages, and in independent testing it scores around 89.6% on naturalness, the best in the field. That is why it leads on voice realism at 9.7 and language support at 9.8. When I need one tool for polished narration, dubbing, and cloning that just sounds right, it is the safe answer. Inworld TTS 1.5 Max ties it on overall score and is the pick when latency matters most alongside quality, its 9.8 latency makes it a genuine real-time contender that still sounds natural. Cartesia Sonic 3 is the latency king outright at a perfect 10, roughly 82ms end to end, so for live voice agents where every millisecond of lag is felt, it is my first call. Hume AI Octave 2 owns emotional range at 9.7 and is the choice when a voice needs to convey feeling rather than just read words. Fish Audio and MiniMax keep the value and multilingual lanes strong, with Fish scoring a 9.8 on value. The clearest market split this year is between batch narration tools like ElevenLabs and WellSaid and real-time agent tools like Cartesia and Murf, whose Falcon model now runs at 55ms. My guidance: ElevenLabs for produced content, Cartesia or Inworld for live agents, Hume when emotion carries the message.

en.commentary: ElevenLabs and Inworld TTS-1.5 Max share the top score at 9.4 and they win on different axes, so I will be direct about which one to pick. ElevenLabs remains the choice for content: voice realism across a wide range of speaking styles, the deepest language coverage, and a library that lets you find a usable voice quickly rather than tuning one for an hour. Inworld TTS-1.5 Max is the choice for products: its latency profile is what makes real time conversational interfaces feel like conversations rather than turn based exchanges. If you are building a voice agent, latency is the factor your users will judge you on, and a 200 millisecond difference is more noticeable than a small step up in timbre. Cartesia Sonic 3 at third is the value play for streaming applications, and Hume AI Octave 2 at fourth is the one I recommend when emotional range is the point, for audio drama, guided meditation and character work. The market context worth noting is that voice is now the fastest moving interface layer in AI products, and pricing is competitive enough that per character costs rarely decide the purchase. Pick on latency if you are shipping an interactive product, and pick on realism plus language coverage if you are producing finished audio. Those two use cases have genuinely different winners.

highlights.title: ElevenLabs for produced audio, Inworld for interactive products
highlights.body: Both sit at 9.4 and they earn it differently. ElevenLabs gives the widest voice library and language coverage, which is what finished narration needs. Inworld's latency profile is what makes a voice agent feel conversational. Deciding between them is really deciding which of those two jobs you have.

highlights.title: Latency beats timbre when users are talking to your product
highlights.body: In a real time voice interface, a 200 millisecond delay is more noticeable to a user than a small improvement in voice quality. People forgive a slightly synthetic tone. They do not forgive waiting. If you are building an agent, rank latency above realism and the choice gets simple.

highlights.title: Hume AI Octave 2 is the pick when emotion carries the content
highlights.body: Audio drama, guided meditation and character work need a voice that can shift register believably. Octave 2 handles emotional range better than the models optimised for neutral narration. For that specific category of content, it produces takes I would keep rather than takes I would regenerate.

highlights.title: Per character pricing rarely decides this purchase any more
highlights.body: Competition has pushed rates close enough together that cost per character is a rounding error against the time you spend tuning voices or working around latency. I score value, and it still matters, though I would not let a 15 percent price gap override a clear fit on latency or language support.

en.commentary: The one genuinely relevant launch this week came from xAI, which released Grok STT 1.0 on July 23. That is speech to text rather than synthesis, so it sits on the other side of this category, and I have left the ranking unchanged. It is still worth understanding, because the voice stack is converging. The tools that win from here will do recognition, synthesis, and cloning in one place with one billing relationship, and a serious new transcription model from a frontier lab is a signal about where that consolidation is heading. My scoring priorities are unchanged and I will defend them. Naturalness of prosody beats raw audio fidelity, because a clean recording of a voice with wrong emphasis is more distracting to a listener than a slightly compressed recording of a voice that phrases correctly. Pronunciation control matters more than the demo reel suggests, since every real project has proper nouns, product names, or acronyms the model will get wrong, and the ability to fix one word without regenerating the paragraph is what makes a tool usable on a deadline. On cloning, my position stays firm: get documented consent from the person whose voice you are replicating, keep the record, and use a platform with a real verification step. The technology is past the point where the ethics are optional, and the platforms with strict consent flows are the ones that will still be operating when the regulation lands.

highlights.title: Prosody beats fidelity and it is not close
highlights.body: A pristine recording of a voice that stresses the wrong word in a sentence pulls a listener straight out of the content. A slightly compressed recording that phrases naturally disappears into the background the way good narration should. I score for rhythm, emphasis, and breath placement ahead of bitrate, because that is what determines whether people finish listening.

highlights.title: Per-word pronunciation control is what makes these usable under deadline
highlights.body: Every real script has a product name, a place, or an acronym the model will mispronounce. The tools that let you fix one word with a phonetic override, without regenerating the surrounding paragraph, save an hour on a long piece. This is the feature I would test first with your own brand names before you subscribe.

highlights.title: Consent for voice cloning is a requirement, and I will keep saying so
highlights.body: Get documented permission from the person whose voice you are replicating and keep the record. Choose a platform with an actual verification step in its cloning flow. Regulation in this area is tightening, and the services with strict consent processes today are the ones that will still be running your project in two years.

highlights.title: Grok STT 1.0 on July 23 signals where the voice stack is heading
highlights.body: xAI shipping a serious speech-to-text model tells you the frontier labs are building the full voice pipeline rather than picking a side. I expect recognition, synthesis, and cloning to consolidate into single platforms with one billing relationship, which favours the vendors already offering both directions over the specialists doing only synthesis.

zh-tw.commentary:
這禮拜唯一真的跟這個品類相關的發表來自 xAI，7 月 23 日推出的 Grok STT 1.0。那是語音轉文字，站在這個品類的另一側，所以排名我維持不動。

不過這件事還是值得理解，因為整個語音技術堆疊正在收斂。接下來會贏的工具，是能在同一個地方、同一組帳單關係下同時做辨識、合成跟複製的那些，而一間前沿實驗室認真推出轉錄模型，就是在告訴你這場整合往哪個方向走。

我的評分優先順序沒變，而且我會替它辯護。語調自然度贏過音質純度，因為一段錄得很乾淨但重音放錯的語音，對聽眾的干擾遠大於一段稍微被壓縮但斷句正確的語音。

發音控制的重要性比 demo 影片讓你以為的高得多，因為每個真實案子都有專有名詞、產品名或縮寫會被念錯，而「能改一個字而不用整段重生」這件事，才是讓工具在趕稿時真的能用的關鍵。

聲音複製這塊我立場不變：跟被複製的當事人拿到書面同意，留存紀錄，選有實際驗證流程的平台。這個技術早就過了「倫理可以先放一邊」的階段，而今天就把同意流程做嚴的平台，才是法規落地之後還活著的那些。

highlights.title: 語調贏過音質，而且差距不小
highlights.body: 一段錄得很乾淨但把重音放在錯字上的語音，會把聽眾直接從內容裡拉出來。一段稍微壓縮過但斷句自然的語音，反而會像好的旁白一樣融進背景裡。我在節奏、重音、換氣位置上給的分數高於位元率，因為那才是決定聽眾聽不聽得完的東西。

highlights.title: 逐字發音控制才是趕稿時真正能救你的功能
highlights.body: 每一份真實腳本都有產品名、地名或縮寫會被念錯。能用音標覆寫修掉單一個字、又不用重生整段的工具，在長篇內容上直接省下一小時。這是我建議你訂閱前拿自家品牌名去測的第一個功能。

highlights.title: 聲音複製的同意權是必要條件，我會一直講
highlights.body: 跟被複製聲音的當事人拿到書面授權，並且留存紀錄。挑選複製流程裡真的有驗證步驟的平台。這個領域的法規正在收緊，今天就把同意流程做嚴的服務，才是兩年後還在幫你跑專案的那幾家。

highlights.title: 7 月 23 日的 Grok STT 1.0 透露了語音堆疊的走向
highlights.body: xAI 認真推出一個語音轉文字模型，等於告訴你前沿實驗室要做的是完整的語音管線，不是選邊站。我預期辨識、合成、複製會整合進同一個平台、同一組帳單關係，這對已經雙向都做的廠商有利，對只做合成的專門戶不利。

en.commentary: ElevenLabs and Inworld TTS-1.5 Max stay tied at the top, and they win on different axes that both matter. ElevenLabs holds first on voice quality and cloning fidelity, producing speech with breath, hesitation, and emphasis that survives close listening on headphones. For audiobook narration and character work where a listener spends hours with one voice, that naturalness is the deciding factor. Inworld TTS-1.5 Max matches it on score by leading on latency and cost at scale, which makes it the better engine behind a live conversational product where round trip time shapes the experience. Cartesia Sonic 3 holds third with the lowest latency in the category, and I recommend it for real time agents where a delay of a few hundred milliseconds breaks the illusion of conversation. Hume AI Octave 2 sits fourth and leads on emotional expressiveness. Alibaba released Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS Plus on July 20, which continues the pattern of the open ecosystem closing ground on hosted providers. Pick by workload: long form narration goes to ElevenLabs, live agents go to Cartesia or Inworld, and emotional range goes to Hume.

highlights.title: ElevenLabs wins where a listener spends hours with one voice
highlights.body: Breath, hesitation, and natural emphasis survive close listening on headphones, which is what audiobook narration and character work demand. Over a multi hour listen, small unnaturalness compounds into fatigue, and this is the engine that avoids it best.

highlights.title: For live agents, latency outranks voice quality
highlights.body: A few hundred milliseconds of delay breaks the sense of conversation more than a slightly synthetic timbre does. Cartesia Sonic 3 delivers the lowest latency in the category, which makes it the right engine behind a real time voice product even against more natural sounding alternatives.

highlights.title: The open audio ecosystem keeps closing ground
highlights.body: Alibaba shipped Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS Plus on July 20, continuing a pattern where open and lower cost options reach quality levels that were exclusive to hosted providers a year ago. For high volume workloads, evaluating those options before signing a large contract is now worth the time.

en.commentary:
The EU AI Act Article 50 enforcement that began on August 2 lands squarely on this category. Synthetic speech distributed to EU audiences now requires machine-readable disclosure, and for anyone producing audiobooks, podcast inserts or advertising for European markets that is a compliance obligation with real consequences. Check what your provider embeds before your next delivery.

ElevenLabs and Inworld TTS 1.5 Max sit tied at the top and they earn it differently. ElevenLabs has the deepest voice library and the most mature cloning pipeline, and its multilingual output holds the speaker's timbre across languages in a way that still surprises me. For audiobook and long-form narration work it remains the default.

Inworld TTS 1.5 Max wins on latency under real-time conditions, which matters enormously for anyone building conversational agents. Sub-200ms time to first audio changes whether an interaction feels like a conversation or a transaction.

Cartesia Sonic 3 at third is the one I point developers toward when cost at scale is the constraint. It delivers most of the quality of the top two at a price that makes high-volume applications viable.

Hume AI Octave 2 at fourth deserves attention for a specific reason: emotional range. Most synthetic speech now sounds human when reading neutral copy. Octave handles a line that needs genuine warmth or hesitation better than the field, which matters for character work and narrative content where flat delivery breaks the illusion immediately.

highlights.title: Article 50 enforcement makes disclosure a delivery requirement
highlights.body: Since August 2, synthetic speech distributed to EU audiences requires machine-readable disclosure under the AI Act. If you produce audiobooks, podcast inserts, IVR systems or advertising reaching European listeners, this is now a compliance obligation with real penalties. Confirm what provenance data your provider embeds before your next delivery, because retrofitting disclosure onto already-published audio is considerably more painful than getting it right upfront.

highlights.title: ElevenLabs holds timbre across languages, which is genuinely hard
highlights.body: Clone a voice in English and generate Mandarin output, and most systems produce something that sounds like a different person. ElevenLabs preserves the speaker's timbre across language boundaries better than anything else I have compared, and for audiobook production, localised training material and any project shipping in multiple languages, that consistency is the whole ballgame. It stays tied at the top on this strength alone.

highlights.title: Inworld wins on latency, and latency decides conversational agents
highlights.body: Time to first audio below 200 milliseconds is the threshold where a spoken exchange starts to feel like a conversation. Inworld TTS 1.5 Max holds that consistently under real load, which is why it ties for first despite a smaller voice library. If you are building a voice agent, latency outranks catalogue depth by a wide margin, because a beautiful voice that arrives half a second late still feels like a machine.

highlights.title: Hume Octave 2 handles emotion the rest of the field flattens
highlights.body: Nearly every model in this category now sounds human reading neutral copy, so that no longer separates anyone. Give the model a line requiring genuine warmth, hesitation or restrained frustration, and most flatten it into pleasant neutrality. Octave 2 carries those emotional beats convincingly, which matters enormously for character work, narrative fiction and any content where flat delivery breaks the illusion in the first sentence.

Inworld TTS-1.5 Max 靠的是 9.8 分延遲加上 9.6 分擬真度。做即時應用，例如接電話的語音代理人，這個組合正好就是你需要的。

Cartesia Sonic 3 的延遲是滿分 10.0，是這份榜單裡唯一拿到滿分的。如果你在做對話式代理人，回應延遲一長幻覺就破了，那就從這裡開始。

Hume AI Octave 2 的情感表現 9.7 分最高。有聲書旁白跟角色配音這種語氣本身就帶意義的工作，表現力就是分水嶺。

CP 值方面，OpenAudio S1 有 9.8 分、GPT-4o mini TTS 有 9.6 分，大量旁白、每分鐘成本會累積的案子，這兩個都很合理。

這週不動。

highlights.title: ElevenLabs 贏在語言廣度
highlights.body: 9.8 分的語言支援是這份榜單最高的，代表同一個聲音身分可以橫跨中文、日文、英文跟數十種語言。台灣創作者要做雙語內容，複製一個聲音然後兩種語言都用，這個工作流程只有在覆蓋真的夠深的時候才成立。

highlights.title: 唯一延遲拿滿分的是 Cartesia Sonic 3
highlights.body: 延遲 10.0 分代表回應速度快到讓語音代理人聽起來像在對話。電話客服或即時助理這種場景，延遲超過幾百毫秒互動感就斷了。要做即時產品，我會用 Cartesia 當基礎。

highlights.title: 語氣最有戲的是 Hume AI Octave 2
highlights.body: 9.7 分情感表現是這裡最高的，在長篇旁白上特別明顯，因為平板的語調聽久了真的很累。有聲書、角色對白、任何情緒本身就承載意義的內容，Octave 2 唸出來的東西聽眾會願意一路聽下去。
